name: Chemical Fertilizers
description: Iran's fertilizer industry connects chemical manufacturing with agricultural nutrient supply. Historical FAO research documents both diversified domestic production and problems of nutrient imbalance, showing why manufacturing output and effective fertilizer use must be assessed separately. [s1][s2]

seo.title: Chemical Fertilizers in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore Iran's fertilizer manufacturing, agricultural distribution and historical nutrient-balance challenges, with explicit limits on current evidence.

content.heading: A manufacturing sector with an agricultural purpose
content.content:
Chemical fertilizers belong to Iran's chemical industries, but their significance extends beyond the factory gate. They supply plant nutrients to agriculture, and their usefulness depends on the composition, availability and application of those nutrients. FAO's historical country study distinguishes nitrogen fertilizers, phosphate fertilizers, potassium products and compound formulations rather than treating fertilizer as a single interchangeable material. [s1]

The distinction also matters statistically. FAOSTAT's nutrient dataset reports nitrogen as N, phosphorus as P₂O₅ and potassium as K₂O. These are nutrient reporting conventions: a tonne of a fertilizer product is not automatically a tonne of the nutrient it contains. Production, imports and agricultural use therefore need clearly defined units before they can be compared. [s3]

content.heading: From early production to a broader product range
content.content:
FAO traces Iranian fertilizer production to a small factory near Karaj in 1945. Its account subsequently describes the development of larger chemical operations, including Razi Petrochemical Industries, and the expansion of private manufacturing into compound fertilizers and micronutrient products. These are historical developments, not evidence of the operating condition of individual plants today. [s1]

The study records products including urea, ammonium phosphates, superphosphates and sulphur-coated urea. It also describes production of zinc, copper, manganese and iron sulphates, alongside boric acid. This range shows why a description limited to bulk nitrogen fertilizer would miss part of the industry's agricultural function. The same report identifies unstable demand and purchasing programmes as difficulties for smaller manufacturers, illustrating the connection between industrial scheduling and agricultural procurement. [s1]

content.heading: Why more fertilizer is not the same as better nutrition
content.content:
FAO's assessment of earlier decades found that rising fertilizer consumption had accompanied an imbalance among nutrients. It described phosphorus accumulation in major farming areas, reduced availability of certain micronutrients, and insufficient potassium replacement relative to crop uptake. It also reported improvements in nutrient balance from the mid-1990s. These findings describe the period studied; they do not establish present conditions throughout Iran. [s2]

Regional variation is central to that assessment. The report presents different recommendations for crops and provinces, including rice-growing areas along the Caspian coast and wheat-producing regions elsewhere. It discusses rainfall and other production practices alongside fertilizer use, cautioning against attributing changes in agricultural output to fertilizer alone. Its recommendations are historical research evidence, not current application instructions for a particular farm. [s2]

content.heading: What a current assessment must establish
content.content:
A defensible contemporary account needs to separate manufacturing output, trade, distribution and agricultural use. FAOSTAT maintains separate product and nutrient datasets, with fertilizer questionnaires and trade statistics among the documented inputs. Those datasets provide a framework for further research, but their existence alone does not verify any particular Iranian observation. [s3][s4]

The historical evidence establishes a diversified industry and a longstanding concern with balanced nutrition. Establishing its present scale requires inspected annual observations and recent operating evidence; neither old production figures nor earlier demand forecasts can serve as current measurements. [s1][s2]

name: Detergents
description: Iran's cleaning-products industry includes laundry powders, dishwashing liquids, soaps and other household formulations. Historical research traces its roots in soap manufacture, while trade documentation and company catalogues show its overlap with personal-care manufacturing. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Detergents and Cleaning Products in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Discover the historical roots and product diversity of Iran's cleaning-products industry, from soap manufacture to household and personal-care brands.

content.heading: Several industries meet on the household shelf
content.content:
Iran's detergent sector is best understood through distinct product groups. The Trade Promotion Organization of Iran's directory lists laundry powders, dishwashing liquids, washing liquids and soaps, alongside bleach and personal-care products. Its company entries show that manufacturers may participate in several of these categories. That commercial overlap does not make the products identical or justify combining all their output into a single detergent statistic. [s2]

The directory also identifies specialized dishwasher products, including tablets, rinse aids and regenerating salt. Its breadth is useful evidence of product differentiation. As an undated directory, however, it cannot establish which listed factories remain operational, which formulations are currently available or how much each producer sells. [s2]

content.heading: Soap making before packaged detergents
content.content:
Historian Willem Floor's account in Encyclopaedia Iranica documents a long history of soap manufacture in Persia. Production was dispersed among towns and workshops rather than beginning with modern consumer-goods factories. In the Qajar period, towns and villages maintained local soap-making traditions. [s1]

The account describes growing interest in imported, perfumed and attractively wrapped soap, followed by attempts to modernize domestic manufacture. A toilet-soap plant established in Tehran did not immediately displace traditional workshops. Later industrial development expanded the product landscape to synthetic detergents and other cleaning preparations. The historical lesson is gradual diversification: older manufacturing practices and newer factory products coexisted, rather than changing in a single nationwide transition. [s1]

content.heading: Household cleaning and personal care
content.content:
Pakrokh's English-language website provides one company example of the industry's broader hygiene setting. It traces the business to Dr. Hamidi Laboratory in 1963 and names brands including Latifeh, Iren, Silvergate and Korend. Its product navigation includes shampoos and hair conditioners. These details document how the company presents its history and range; its claims about market standing are not independent measurements. [s3]

This example helps explain a recurring classification problem. A manufacturer described broadly as a hygiene-products business may sell products used on clothing, household surfaces, hair or skin. Research must identify the particular product before assigning production, sales or trade figures to detergents. A brand list can establish examples of commercial activity, but cannot by itself establish national market size. [s2][s3]

content.heading: Understanding the sector beyond brand familiarity
content.content:
The inspected sources connect a familiar consumer category with a longer manufacturing history. Iranica supplies historical context; the trade directory records a differentiated industrial product range; and a company website illustrates branded personal-care activity. Together they support a qualitative account, with different limits for each kind of evidence. [s1][s2][s3]

A current industrial assessment still requires comparable production and trade records by product. It also needs independent evidence before making claims about cleaning performance, environmental advantages or market leadership. The available material supports describing the sector's diversity, while leaving its current scale and the performance of individual products unresolved. [s2][s3]

name: Paints & Resins
description: Iranian manufacturers document a range of coating products and resin families, including alkyd, acrylic and unsaturated polyester materials. Company portfolios show connections among paint manufacture, automotive repair, composites and other downstream industries, although they do not establish national production totals. [s1][s2][s3]

seo.title: Paints, Coatings and Resins in Iran | Iran, Unfolded
seo.description: Explore documented Iranian paint and resin manufacturing, its regional examples and connections with coatings, automotive repair and composites.

content.heading: Related products with different industrial roles
content.content:
Iran's paints and resins sector includes companies supplying finished coatings and companies supplying materials to downstream manufacturers. Rakhshan Resin Tehran, for example, describes operations spanning industrial paints, alkyd resins and unsaturated polyester resins. Simab Resin presents a different emphasis: water-based acrylic resins and polyurethane resins supplied across several industries. [s1][s2]

These portfolios show why the sector cannot be understood simply as the manufacture of wall paint. Resin suppliers can serve markets outside coatings, while a coatings business may produce several chemically distinct product families. Company catalogues help identify that breadth, but do not reveal the national balance between the different activities. [s1][s2]

content.heading: Manufacturing examples across industrial regions
content.content:
Rakhshan Resin Tehran says it began activities in 2000 and obtained an operating licence for production in Eshtehard Industrial Park, in Alborz province. It describes subsequent expansion of its product range to include orthophthalic and isophthalic unsaturated polyester resins. Its catalogue also distinguishes alkyd, epoxy and polyurethane coating categories. These are manufacturer-reported details rather than an independent plant audit. [s1]

Simab Resin places its factory in Kaveh Industrial City near Saveh and dates the start of operations to 1991. Petro Octane Isatis identifies factories in Yazd province and lists polyester and vinylester resins, alkyd resins, putties and paint driers. Together these examples demonstrate activity beyond a single manufacturing location, without establishing a complete national map or ranking industrial clusters. [s2][s3]

content.heading: Where coatings and other material industries overlap
content.content:
Yashm's Persian-language website provides an example of a business combining industrial coatings, automotive refinish products, wood coatings and resins. Automotive refinish refers to coatings used in vehicle repair and repainting. The company lists primers, intermediate coats, two-component topcoats and putties, illustrating the different products within a repair-coating system. [s4]

Its resin descriptions also identify applications involving pipes and composite manufacturing. Simab's categories extend further, including textiles, paper, printing and packaging, leather and pressure-sensitive adhesives. The useful distinction is between a resin's chemical family and the application for which a particular grade is supplied: a broad family name alone does not establish that products are interchangeable. [s2][s4]

content.heading: What catalogues establish—and what remains open
content.content:
The inspected catalogues establish a documented range of Iranian commercial offerings. They also show specialization: Isatis lists paint driers and additives alongside resins, while Simab emphasizes water-based materials and several downstream markets. This is evidence of product positioning, rather than proof of market leadership, independently verified performance or the scale of domestic substitution for imports. [s2][s3]

A stronger contemporary assessment would connect these product descriptions with inspected production records, input sourcing and independent technical evidence. Company expansion histories cannot substitute for annual output, and individual portfolios cannot establish national demand. The supported conclusion is a diverse manufacturing field whose current scale and performance still require further research. [s1][s2][s3][s4]
